claim: A GPU energy study found online-serving inference workloads spend 61% of in-execution time in an execution-idle state, consuming 48% of total energy during those idle intervals.
stance_target: idle agent compute is a major, measurable cost/energy driver that justifies aggressive auto-termination or suspension policies
scope_conditions: GPU-backed online serving workloads, closest proxy to agent patterns per source
quoted_support: A GPU cluster energy study measured that online serving workloads spent 61% of in-execution time in an execution-idle state, with 48% of energy consumed during those intervals.

claim: Real-world infrastructure audits show average compute utilization often below 20%, meaning most provisioned agent/sandbox capacity sits idle.
stance_target: idle agent/compute waste is pervasive in production, not an edge case
quoted_support: Real-world infrastructure audits show average utilization often hovers below 20%.

claim: Major cloud serverless platforms (GCP Cloud Run, Azure Functions Flex Consumption) enforce minimum billing periods or charge for always-ready idle instances, meaning idle agent time is billed as if active under standard duration-based pricing.
stance_target: standard cloud billing models do not naturally reward killing idle agents quickly; idle-shutdown policy must be deliberately engineered
scope_conditions: GCP Cloud Run and Azure Functions Flex Consumption billing models
quoted_support: GCP Cloud Run enforces a 1-minute minimum per instance under instance-based billing. Azure Functions Flex Consumption charges $0.000004 per GB-second for always-ready instances, even when idle.

claim: Blaxel's sandbox platform transitions agent sandboxes to a zero-compute-cost standby state after 15 seconds of network inactivity, and resumes from standby in under 25 milliseconds with full prior state restored via microVM isolation.
stance_target: implementation pattern for fast idle-suspend / fast-resume as an alternative to full self-termination
quoted_support: Blaxel bill by the GB-second and transition sandboxes to standby after 15 seconds of network inactivity. In standby mode, only storage costs for the snapshot and volumes continue to accrue. Compute charges cease entirely. ... resume from standby in under 25 milliseconds with the previous state restored.

claim: Traditional sandbox providers (CodeSandbox, E2B, Daytona) keep instances running for up to 10-15 minutes by default after activity stops, producing compute costs up to 5x higher than aggressive idle-suspend approaches for users who don't manually manage lifecycle.
stance_target: default idle-timeout settings on competing sandbox platforms are too conservative, leaving substantial idle-billing waste if not explicitly overridden
scope_conditions: CodeSandbox, E2B, Daytona sandbox platforms (vendor-comparison claim)
quoted_support: Traditional sandbox providers such as CodeSandbox, E2B, and Daytona keep instances running for up to 10 or 15 minutes by default. This means that users that are not scrupulous about manually managing the lifecycle will receive compute costs for every session of every sandbox, resulting in compute costs that can be up to 5 times higher.

claim: Container restart / re-initialization overhead for AI agent workloads consumes 31-48% of total task time when sandbox state is not persisted between sessions.
stance_target: aggressive self-termination without state persistence imposes a large re-initialization cost penalty on resumed agents
quoted_support: Container restart overhead for AI agent workloads consumes 31-48% of total task time according to measured benchmarks.

claim: AWS research documents a 37% performance gap between lab and production conditions for agentic multi-agent systems, which inflates the effective per-task cost of agent failures that must be retried or escalated.
stance_target: idle/failure-detection logic in production agent fleets must account for a substantial lab-to-production reliability gap
scope_conditions: AWS-documented multi-agent systems in production vs lab
quoted_support: AWS research on multi-agent systems documents a 37% performance gap between lab and production conditions for agentic systems.
